sections.b: Joshua is the book where the ban (cherem) is carried out. Jericho is put under the ban entirely, except Rahab's household and the metals given to the LORD (Joshua 6:17–24). Achan's theft of banned goods makes Israel itself "something under the ban" until he is destroyed (Joshua 7:11–12). At Ai the people are banned but Israel may keep the livestock and plunder (Joshua 8:2, 26–27). The southern and northern campaigns repeat the formula "he left no survivor" and "everything that breathed" (Joshua 10:28–40; Joshua 11:11–14), citing Deuteronomy 20:16–17. Yet two Canaanite groups survive by oath, Rahab and the Gibeonites (Joshua 2; Joshua 9), and 11:20 says that no town except Gibeon sought peace because God hardened their hearts.
sections.refs: Joshua 6:17–24; Joshua 7:11–12; Joshua 8:2; Joshua 8:26–27; Joshua 10:28–40; Joshua 11:11–20; Deuteronomy 20:16–17

sections.b: Many scholars of every school point out that Joshua's own text qualifies its sweeping claims. Joshua "took the whole land" (11:23), but "very much of the land" remains (13:1). Hebron and Debir are wiped out (10:36–39) and must be taken again (15:13–17; Judges 1:10–15). Jerusalem's king is killed (10:23–26), but the Jebusites stay (15:63). K. Lawson Younger compared Assyrian, Hittite and Egyptian war reports, which describe total destruction in stock phrases while other records show the enemy surviving. On this reading, "all" and "no survivor" belong to a style of victory report. Others answer that the style does not remove the moral problem, since the text still presents total killing as God's will.
sections.refs: Joshua 10:36–39; Joshua 11:23; Joshua 13:1; Joshua 15:13–17; Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:10–15

sections.h: Judgment, expulsion and room to repent
sections.b: Readers who see the conquest as a unique judgment stress that the land's people lost it for their deeds, not their race. Abraham's descendants must wait because "the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (Genesis 15:16), and Israel is warned that the land will vomit it out too if it does the same things (Leviticus 18:24–28; Deuteronomy 8:19–20), which the exile later fulfilled. The Wisdom of Solomon adds that God judged the Canaanites little by little, giving them room to repent (Wisdom 12:3–11). Others argue from the verbs: the main commands are to "drive out" and "take possession" (garash, yarash; Exodus 23:28–30; Numbers 33:52; Deuteronomy 7:20), slowly and with the hornet's help, while the ban falls mainly on fortified royal towns. On this reading, by Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan and by John and Harvey Walton, the aim was to remove a people and its worship from the land, not to kill every person.
sections.refs: Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 18:24–28; Deuteronomy 8:19–20; Wisdom 12:3–11; Exodus 23:28–30; Numbers 33:52; Deuteronomy 7:20

sections.b: Deuteronomy 20 tells Israel to offer peace to a town before attacking it (20:10–15), then says the towns of the land itself are to be put under the ban (20:16–18). Jewish tradition reads this in two ways. The Sifre and Rashi limit the offer of peace to distant towns, so the seven nations of Canaan were not offered terms. Nachmanides held that peace was offered to every town, and the Jerusalem Talmud says that Joshua sent word ahead: whoever wants to leave, leave; whoever wants peace, make peace; whoever wants war, make war (Shevi'it 6:1). Maimonides ruled that peace must be offered even to the seven nations, on condition that they keep the seven Noahide laws and accept tribute and service (Laws of Kings 6:1–5). On this reading, Joshua 11:19–20 means that the towns refused.

common: Most critical scholars and archaeologists think the campaigns did not happen as told: the stories were written centuries later to teach total loyalty to the LORD.
Most traditional Jewish and Christian readers: the ban in Joshua was a unique judgment on Canaan's sin, not a pattern for later wars.
Ancient war reports used total language that was not meant to be taken literally.
uncommon: Rahab and the Gibeonites show that the book itself questions the ban.
The ban is best read only as a picture of the soul's war against sin, as Origen read it.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the ban framed by two oaths
claude.body: My own observation: the first conquest story (Jericho) is framed by an oath to a Canaanite (Rahab, 2:12–14), and the last major story before the campaigns (Gibeon, 9:15–20) is another oath to Canaanites. In both cases Israel's sworn word overrides the ban. I suggest that the book deliberately places the ban inside a frame of covenant loyalty, so that the reader learns that God's people are bound first by faithfulness to their word and to God, and only then by the command to destroy. Many scholars note the Rahab-Gibeon parallel; reading it as an intentional frame around the ban is my own proposal.

sections.b: Joshua 1–12 shows Joshua as a second Moses. God promises to be with him as with Moses (Joshua 1:5; Joshua 3:7). He sends spies, leads a crossing of water, and is made great in Israel's eyes (Joshua 4:14). He meets the commander of the LORD's army and is told to remove his sandal, as Moses was (Joshua 5:15; Exodus 3:5). He intercedes after defeat (Joshua 7:6–9), holds out his javelin until Ai falls, like Moses' raised hands (Joshua 8:18, 26; Exodus 17:11–12), writes and reads the law (Joshua 8:30–35), and commands the sun and moon (Joshua 10:12). The first half of the book closes: "As the LORD had commanded his servant Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did" (Joshua 11:15).
sections.refs: Joshua 1:5; Joshua 3:7; Joshua 4:14; Joshua 5:13–15; Joshua 7:6–9; Joshua 8:18–26; Joshua 8:30–35; Joshua 10:12–14; Joshua 11:15

common: Joshua's Hebrew name is the same as Jesus' name, Yeshua.

sections.b: Rahab hides the spies under flax on her roof, misleads the king's men, and speaks the fullest confession of faith in the book: "the LORD your God, he is God in the sky above and on the earth below" (Joshua 2:11), the words of Deuteronomy 4:39. She asks for loyal love (hesed) for her family, and the spies swear to spare all who stay in her house under the scarlet cord (Joshua 2:12–21). When Jericho falls, the spies bring out her whole family, and she "has lived among Israel to this day" (Joshua 6:22–25). Her story is the mirror image of Achan's in Joshua 7: the Canaanite insider to faith is saved, the Israelite who breaks faith is destroyed.

Josephus and the Targum softened her trade to innkeeper, but the Hebrew zonah and the Greek of the New Testament mean prostitute. The rabbis made her a righteous convert, Joshua's wife and ancestor of eight prophets and priests, including Jeremiah (Bavli Megillah 14b). Clement of Rome saw the scarlet cord as a sign of redemption through Christ's blood (1 Clement 12). Augustine and Calvin judged her lie a fault forgiven by grace, while many later Christians defended it as protecting life.
sections.refs: Joshua 2:1; Joshua 2:4–6; Joshua 2:18–21; Matthew 1:5; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25

common: Rahab's scarlet cord points to the blood of Christ.
Rahab was an innkeeper rather than a prostitute.
uncommon: Rahab of Jericho and the Rahab in Matthew 1:5 were different women, since the dates are hard to fit.

sections.b: Jericho was the gateway from the Jordan fords to the hill country. Israel marched around it once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh, with priests blowing ram's horns before the ark; at the shout the wall fell where it stood (Joshua 6:1–20). The town was put under the ban, Rahab's family was saved, and Joshua cursed anyone who would rebuild it (Joshua 6:21–26). Hebrews 11:30 says the walls fell "by faith."

Garstang (1930s) dated a destruction to about 1400 BC; Kenyon (1950s) redated it to about 1550 BC and found almost nothing from the 13th century; radiocarbon dating (1995) supported her. Bryant Wood (1990) defended a date near 1400 BC, which would fit a 15th-century exodus. Most archaeologists hold that Jericho was unwalled or abandoned in the late Bronze Age; those who hold the early date, and those who think erosion removed later remains, read the evidence differently. See also the topic on the date of the Exodus.

Ai is the scene of Israel's first defeat: three thousand men run, thirty-six die, and Israel's heart melts (Joshua 7:2–5). After Achan is found out and punished, God gives Joshua a plan of ambush, and Ai is taken and burned, its twelve thousand people killed and its king hung on a tree until evening (Joshua 8:1–29). Ai, "the ruin," is made "a ruin mound forever" (Joshua 8:28). The site usually identified, et-Tell, was a large Early Bronze city abandoned about 2400 BC and resettled only as a village about 1200 BC. Scholars have proposed an etiological story, a transfer from nearby Bethel, or a different site such as Khirbet el-Maqatir.

Gilgal, "on the east edge of Jericho," is where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and where Joshua set up the twelve stones (Joshua 4:19–20). There the new generation was circumcised, and God said, "Today I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt," a play on the name (Joshua 5:2–9). Israel kept the Passover there and ate the produce of the land, and the manna stopped (Joshua 5:10–12). The Gibeonites came to the camp at Gilgal, and Joshua marched from there to their rescue (Joshua 9:6; Joshua 10:6–9). 4QJosh-a may place the first altar here.
sections.refs: Joshua 4:19–24; Joshua 5:2–12; Joshua 9:6; Joshua 10:6–9; Joshua 10:15; Joshua 10:43

sections.b: Gibeon's people, Hivites from four towns, disguised themselves as travelers from "a far country," the category Deuteronomy 20:15 allowed Israel to make peace with. Israel tasted their bread "but did not ask the LORD what to do," made a covenant and swore an oath (Joshua 9:3–15). When the truth came out, the leaders kept their oath, and Joshua made the Gibeonites woodcutters and water carriers "for the house of my God" (Joshua 9:16–27). Their treaty drew Israel into the war with the five kings, whom God defeated with hail and the long day (Joshua 10:1–14). Only Gibeon made peace with Israel (Joshua 11:19).

common: The Gibeonites' story teaches that promises must be kept even when made by mistake.
uncommon: The story preserves a real early treaty between Israel and a league of Hivite towns.

sections.b: Joshua spoke to the LORD and said, "Sun, be still at Gibeon" (Joshua 10:12). The poem is quoted from the Book of Jashar, followed by prose: the sun "did not hurry to go down for about a whole day" (Joshua 10:13). Readings include a literal halt; a lengthened light; a darkening or eclipse, since dom means "be silent" (Robert Dick Wilson; Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington proposed an eclipse of 1207 BC); a favorable omen of sun and moon (John Walton); and poetry, like Judges 5:20. The text's own emphasis is on prayer: "the LORD listened to a man's voice, for the LORD fought for Israel" (Joshua 10:14).

common: The earth stopped turning for about a day.
uncommon: NASA computers found a "missing day" in time, a modern legend with no basis.
The sun stopped shining, and Joshua prayed for relief from the heat.

sections.b: Jabin king of Hazor gathered the northern kings, a host "as many as the sand on the seashore," at the waters of Merom (Joshua 11:1–5). After the victory Joshua took Hazor, "the head of all these kingdoms," killed its people and burned it, the only northern town he burned (Joshua 11:10–13). Archaeologists found that Canaanite Hazor was destroyed by fire in the 13th century BC, its statues of gods and kings smashed; Yadin and Ben-Tor credited Israel, others an internal revolt. Judges 4 has another Jabin ruling there.

Joshua 3–4 tells the crossing as a second Exodus. The priests carrying the ark stepped into the river in its spring flood, and the water upstream stood "in one heap" at Adam, while the people crossed "on dry ground" (Joshua 3:13–17). Twelve stones taken from the riverbed were set up at Gilgal so that children would ask and parents would tell (Joshua 4:1–9, 20–24). The text makes the link explicit: God did to the Jordan "just as" to the Sea of Reeds (Joshua 4:23). Landslides near Adam (Tell ed-Damiyeh) blocked the river in AD 1267 and 1927, which some take as the means God used.

Joshua's first half is woven from Deuteronomy's words. God's charge to Joshua reuses Deuteronomy 11:24–25 and 31:6–8 (Joshua 1:3–9). Rahab's confession echoes Deuteronomy 4:39 (Joshua 2:11). The ban follows Deuteronomy 7 and 20, the hanging and burial at sunset follow Deuteronomy 21:22–23 (Joshua 8:29; Joshua 10:26–27), the altar and the reading at Ebal follow Deuteronomy 27 (Joshua 8:30–35), and the Gibeonites exploit Deuteronomy 20:15 (Joshua 9:6). For Martin Noth these links showed one author; for traditional readers they show Joshua obeying the book Moses left him.
sections.refs: Joshua 1:3–9; Joshua 2:11; Joshua 8:29–35; Joshua 9:6; Joshua 10:26–27; Joshua 11:15

sections.b: The date of the conquest follows from the date of the Exodus, forty years earlier. On the early date (about 1446 BC) the crossing comes about 1406 BC; supporters point to Bryant Wood's dating of Jericho's fall and to the 'Apiru of the Amarna letters. On the late date (13th century BC) supporters point to the destruction of Hazor and to the Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC), the first mention of Israel outside the Bible. Neither date fits all the sites: Jericho and Ai show little or no occupation in the 13th century, while Hazor's great fire is in the 13th. Many critical scholars conclude that Joshua 1–12 is not a record of a single campaign at all.

Joshua 1 promises the land from the wilderness and "this Lebanon to the great river, the river Euphrates" (Joshua 1:4), echoing Genesis 15:18 and Deuteronomy 11:24. Chapters 2–11 tell how it was taken, and 11:23 says, "Joshua took the whole land... and Joshua gave it as an inheritance to Israel." The book uses two verbs for this: yarash, "take possession," Israel's task, and nachal, "inherit," the land as a gift shared out. Chapter 12 lists thirty-one defeated kings. Yet 13:1 says that much land remained, and the Euphrates border was never reached in Joshua's time.
sections.refs: Joshua 1:2–6; Joshua 1:11; Joshua 11:16–23; Joshua 12:1–24; Joshua 13:1; Genesis 15:18–21

sections.h: The ark at the Jordan and Jericho
sections.b: In Joshua 3–6 the ark is the center of every scene. It goes ahead of the people at a distance of two thousand cubits (Joshua 3:3–4); when the priests' feet touch the Jordan, the river stops (Joshua 3:13–16); the priests stand with it in the riverbed until all have crossed (Joshua 3:17; Joshua 4:10–11). At Jericho it is carried around the town every day, with seven priests and their horns before it (Joshua 6:4–13). After the defeat at Ai, Joshua falls before it (Joshua 7:6), and at Ebal the people stand on both sides of it (Joshua 8:33). It is called "the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth" (Joshua 3:11).

At Gilgal God told Joshua to circumcise Israel "again, a second time," because the generation born in the wilderness had not been circumcised (Joshua 5:2–7). Joshua used flint knives, and the place was called the Hill of Foreskins (Joshua 5:3). God then said, "Today I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt" (Joshua 5:9). The rite came before the Passover, which only the circumcised could eat (Exodus 12:48). The Greek text explains the event differently. Justin Martyr saw in it a picture of Christ's circumcision of the heart (Colossians 2:11).

sections.h: The first Passover in the land
sections.b: Israel crossed the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, the day the Passover lambs were chosen (Joshua 4:19; Exodus 12:3), and kept the Passover at Gilgal on the evening of the fourteenth (Joshua 5:10). The next day they ate the produce of the land, unleavened bread and roasted grain, and the manna stopped (Joshua 5:11–12). Rahab's house, marked with a scarlet cord, with her family inside and death outside, recalls the first Passover night (Joshua 2:18–19; Exodus 12:22–23).

"The manna stopped the next day, once they ate from the produce of the land" (Joshua 5:12). Exodus 16:35 had foretold that the manna would last until Israel reached a settled land. The wilderness lessons of daily dependence (Deuteronomy 8:3) now give way to the test of plenty (Deuteronomy 8:10–18).

sections.h: The stones of Gilgal and the heaps of Joshua
sections.b: Joshua sets up twelve stones from the Jordan at Gilgal and twelve in the riverbed (Joshua 4:3–9, 20). They are memorials, meant to make children ask "What do these stones mean?" (Joshua 4:6, 21). Other heaps of stone in Joshua mark judgment: over Achan (Joshua 7:26), over the king of Ai (Joshua 8:29) and at the mouth of the cave at Makkedah (Joshua 10:27), all "to this day." At Ebal the law is written on stones (Joshua 8:32).
sections.refs: Joshua 4:3–9; Joshua 4:20–24; Joshua 7:26; Joshua 8:29; Joshua 8:32; Joshua 10:27

sections.h: A second Exodus at the Jordan
sections.b: Joshua 1–5 retells the Exodus for a new generation. Rahab reports that Canaan has heard how the LORD dried up the Sea of Reeds (Joshua 2:10), and her words echo Exodus 15:15–16. The Jordan stands up "in one heap" like the sea (Joshua 3:13; Exodus 15:8), and the people cross "on dry ground" (Joshua 3:17; Exodus 14:22). Joshua says plainly that God did to the Jordan "just as" to the Sea of Reeds (Joshua 4:23). Then come circumcision, Passover and an encounter on holy ground, as in Exodus 3–12. Psalm 114 sings both crossings together.
sections.refs: Joshua 2:9–11; Joshua 3:13–17; Joshua 4:23–24; Joshua 5:2–15; Exodus 14:21–22; Exodus 15:8; Psalm 114:3–5

sections.b: Rahab asks the spies to repay her loyal love (hesed) with loyal love to her family, and they promise "loyal love and faithfulness" (Joshua 2:12–14). The pair hesed ve-emet is used of God himself (Exodus 34:6). The story shows hesed as the bond of a covenant, here made across the line between Israel and Canaan.

Joshua's war stories are full of outsiders who join Israel. Rahab confesses the LORD and lives among Israel (Joshua 2:11; Joshua 6:25). At Ebal "the foreigner as well as the native-born" stands with Israel and hears the whole law (Joshua 8:33, 35). The Gibeonites, who heard what the LORD had done, are spared and serve at his altar (Joshua 9:9, 24–27). The wonders at the Jordan were done so that "all the peoples of the earth" would know the LORD (Joshua 4:24). Many readers see the book teaching that faith, not birth, decides who belongs, while others note that the Gibeonites are kept as permanent laborers.

sections.h: The commander of the LORD's army
sections.b: Near Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who says, "No. I am the commander of the LORD's army," and tells him to remove his sandal because the place is holy (Joshua 5:13–15). Jewish tradition often identified him as Michael (compare Daniel 10:13, 21); many church fathers, beginning with Justin Martyr, saw him as the pre-incarnate Word of God, since he lets Joshua bow down before him (the Hebrew verb is also the usual word for worship) and makes the ground holy. Others take him as an angel sent by God, like the angel with a drawn sword who met Balaam (Numbers 22:31).

sections.h: The Anakim and Og in Joshua
sections.b: The Anakim, whose size had frightened the first generation (Numbers 13:33; Deuteronomy 1:28), are cut off from Hebron, Debir, Anab and the hill country, and survive only in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (Joshua 11:21–22). Og of Bashan is remembered as "one of the last of the Rephaim" (Joshua 12:4). Goliath of Gath may be the Bible's memory of those who were left (1 Samuel 17:4).

Their defeat is the news that frightens Canaan: Rahab and the Gibeonites both mention it (Joshua 2:10; Joshua 9:10). Joshua 12 opens its list of defeated kings with them, describing Sihon's land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and Og's from Hermon to Bashan, all given by Moses to the eastern tribes (Joshua 12:1–6).

sections.h: The altar on Ebal and the reading of the law
sections.b: After Ai, Joshua builds an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal, writes a copy of the law on stones, and reads it all, the blessing and the curse, with half the people before Gerizim and half before Ebal (Joshua 8:30–35), fulfilling Deuteronomy 27. The passage stands in three places in three witnesses: after 8:29 in the Hebrew, after 9:2 in the Greek, and after the crossing in 4QJosh-a. Adam Zertal's Iron Age structure on Ebal has been claimed as this altar, a claim others dispute.

sections.h: Joshua and the scroll of the law
sections.b: Joshua is the first leader told to live by a written law: "This scroll of the law must not leave your mouth. Murmur it to yourself day and night" (Joshua 1:8). The book stresses that Joshua does what is "written in the scroll of the law of Moses" (Joshua 8:31), writes a copy of it on stones, and reads every word to all Israel, including women, children and foreigners (Joshua 8:32–35). The first half ends: "He did not leave out a thing from all that the LORD had commanded Moses" (Joshua 11:15).

Joshua twice obeys Deuteronomy 21:22–23 exactly. The king of Ai is hung on a tree until evening and taken down at sunset, and a heap of stones is raised over him (Joshua 8:29). The five kings of the south are killed, hung on five trees until evening, and thrown into the cave at Makkedah at sunset (Joshua 10:26–27). In both cases "hanging" is the display of a body after death.

The Septuagint of Joshua is about four to five percent shorter than the Hebrew and differs in order and wording. It lacks 8:11b–13 and 8:26, 10:15 and 10:43, and the mention of the Book of Jashar (10:13); it tells 5:4–6 differently; it adds the fulfillment of Joshua's curse at 6:26; and it places the altar on Ebal (8:30–35) after 9:2. The Dead Sea Scroll 4QJosh-a puts that passage after the crossing instead. Emanuel Tov and others argue that the Greek often preserves an older Hebrew edition; others think its translator shortened and rearranged.
sections.refs: Joshua 5:4–6; Joshua 6:26; Joshua 8:11–13; Joshua 8:26; Joshua 8:30–35; Joshua 9:2; Joshua 10:13–15; Joshua 10:43

sections.b: Joshua reminds the eastern tribes that "The LORD your God is giving you rest" (Joshua 1:13), and that their brothers must have rest too before they go home (Joshua 1:15). After the northern campaign "the land was quiet, with no more war" (Joshua 11:23). Hebrews 4:8 argues that Joshua's rest was not the final one.

sections.h: Rahab's faith and the walls of Jericho
sections.b: Hebrews 11:30–31 draws two examples of faith from Joshua 2–6: the walls of Jericho fell by faith after seven days of marching, and Rahab did not die with the disobedient because she welcomed the spies. James 2:25 uses Rahab with Abraham to argue that faith shows itself in deeds. In Joshua her faith is a spoken confession (Joshua 2:9–11) joined to risky action (Joshua 2:4–6, 15).

For the crossing, one man is chosen from each tribe, and each carries a stone, "to match the number of the tribes of the Israelites" (Joshua 3:12; Joshua 4:2–8). The eastern tribes, Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, already have their land but must cross armed ahead of their brothers (Joshua 1:12–18; Joshua 4:12–13). The lot that finds Achan goes tribe by tribe, clan by clan (Joshua 7:14–18).

Joshua explains that "it was the LORD's doing to make their hearts stubborn, so that they would meet Israel in battle" (Joshua 11:20). The verb is the one used of Pharaoh (Exodus 4:21; Exodus 14:4). The verse explains why only Gibeon sought peace (Joshua 11:19), and is read alongside Rahab and the Gibeonites, who show that surrender was possible.

Joshua 10:13 quotes the poem about the sun and moon from "the Book of Jashar," a lost collection also cited for David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:18). The Septuagint of Joshua does not mention it. Later books with that name are medieval or modern.
